```{r data-setup, include=FALSE}
colors.opinion <- c("red", "orange", "grey", "cyan", "blue")

colors.red <- "#BA2F2A"
colors.green <- "#088158"

scale_defender <- scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Defender")
scale_attacker <- scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Attacker")

scale_percentage_bars <- function(dodge_value = 0.9, vjust = -0.2, with.percent = TRUE) {
  list(
  if (with.percent) scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) else scale_y_continuous(),
  geom_col(position = "dodge"),
  geom_text(
    aes(label = if(with.percent) percent(after_stat(y), accuracy = 0.1) else round(after_stat(y), digits = 2)),
    position = position_dodge(dodge_value), 
    vjust = vjust
    )
  )
}

# Groups by llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human and cut,
scale_default_grouping <- function(type) {
  if (! type %in% c("t", "m")) {
    stop("type must be t or m")
  }
  list(
    aes(x = author_llm_or_human, fill = opponent_llm_or_human),
    facet_wrap( ~ cut),
    labs(x = ifelse(type == "t", "Defender", "Attacker"), 
         fill = ifelse(type == "t", "Attacker", "Defender"),)
    
  )
}

binary_mean_cols <- function(.data, y, type, with.percent = TRUE) {
  .data |>
    summarise(
      {{y}} := mean({{y}}),
      .by = c(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, cut)
    ) |>
    ggplot(aes(y = {{y}})) +
    scale_default_grouping(type) +
    scale_percentage_bars(with.percent = with.percent)
}

# Returns a df where all specified columns are normalised to a value between
# 0 and 1
normalise <- function(.data, ...) {
  cols <- enquos(...)
  .data |>
    mutate(across(c(!!!cols), function(p) {
      p <- as.numeric(p)
      (p - min(p, na.rm = TRUE)) / (max(p, na.rm = TRUE) - min(p, na.rm = TRUE))
      }
      ))
}

# Utility functions for displaying results from regression models

estimate <- function(model, coeff_name) {
  round(model$coefficients[coeff_name, "Estimate"], digits = 4)
}

p.value <- function(model, coeff_name) {
  round(model$coefficients[coeff_name, "Pr(>|t|)"], digits = 4)
}

r.sq <- function(model) {
  percent(model$r.squared, accuracy = 0.01)
}

```

# Human skill levels

NOTE: I don't think this is really useful, after all. 
There are only 24 players, so there are only 12 players for each role.
Dividing these into two groups based on skill level leaves only 6 players in
each role, with only a very dodgy theoretical
reasoning as to why this classification should matter at all. Further grouping -
by opponent or CuT, for example - would lead to groups with only a single player,
or no player at all. ENDNOTE

In the questionnaire, study participants could enter their semester, their
experience with Java and JUnit, respectively, and they had to answer a short
single-choice
quiz with JUnit-related questions.

```{r}
questionnaire |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      java_experience, 
      junit_experience
      ),
    names_to = "xp_type",
    values_to = "xp_value"
    ) |>
  mutate(xp_type = recode_values(
    xp_type,
    "java_experience" ~ "Java experience",
    "junit_experience" ~ "JUnit experience"
  )) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(xp_type, xp_value)) |>
  
  ggplot(aes(x = xp_type, y = n, fill = xp_value)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  geom_text(aes(label = after_stat(y)), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(fill = "Experience", x = NULL, y = "Count", 
       title = "Experience of study participants")

```
```{r}
questionnaire |>
  mutate(number_correct_questions = ordered(number_correct_questions)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(number_correct_questions)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = n, fill = number_correct_questions)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", fill = "Number of correctly answered questions",
       title = "Quiz results")
```

```{r}
questionnaire |>
  mutate(semester = ordered(semester)) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(semester)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = n, fill = semester)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", fill = "Semester",
       title = "Semester of participants")
```

## Skill levels as predictors of submission quality

It might be useful in further analysis to divide users into highly-skilled,
mid-skilled and low-skilled users. We will use a linear regression model to
see if and how these aforementioned variables predict submission quality.

For submission quality, we choose *Kill rate* and *Evasion rate* 
(defined later in the document) as proxies, as they are calculated against
the totality of other mutants/tests and rely less on the highly unpredictable
nature of a single game.


### For tests:
Hypothesis: The number of correctly answered questions, Java experience,
JUnit experience and semester all are positively correlated with Kill rate
for tests. We control for experiment round (practice could increase quality,
or boredom could decrease it), the Class under Test, and whether the opponent 
is an LLM player
or a human.

We normalize the variables for better comparability.

```{r}
testmodel <- deftests |>
  filter(author_llm_or_human == "Human") |>
  normalise(author_number_correct_questions, author_java_experience, author_junit_experience, author_semester) %>%
  lm(data = .,
        kill_rate ~ author_number_correct_questions 
          + author_java_experience
          + author_junit_experience
          + author_semester 
          + round 
          + cut 
          + opponent_llm_or_human
     ) |>
  summary()

testmodel
```

Result: Of the proposed variables, only *JUnit-Experience* has an effect on
_kill rate_ that is significant to a level of 5%. The difference between those
of lowest experience and those of highest experience
increases evasion rate by `r estimate(testmodel, "author_junit_experience")`.

Overall, the model explains
`r r.sq(testmodel)` of the total variation.

### For mutants:

We repeat this procedure for mutants, checking for *evasion rate*.

```{r}

mutantmodel <- mutants |>
  filter(author_llm_or_human == "Human") |>
  normalise(author_number_correct_questions, author_java_experience, author_junit_experience, author_semester) %>%
  lm(data = .,
        evasion_rate ~ author_number_correct_questions 
          + author_java_experience
          + author_junit_experience
          + author_semester 
          + round 
          + cut 
          + opponent_llm_or_human
     ) |>
  summary()

mutantmodel
```

This paints a very different picture than the analysis for tests: The 
_number of correctly answered questions_ is positively correlated to 
_evasion rate_ (`r estimate(mutantmodel, "author_number_correct_questions")`), 
as is _JUnit experience_ (`r estimate(mutantmodel, "author_junit_experience")`). 
_Java Experience_ however is negatively correlated 
(`r estimate(mutantmodel, "author_java_experience")`), as is _semester_
(`r estimate(mutantmodel, "author_semester")`), although _semester_ no longer fits
the significance level of 5% with a p-value of 
`r p.value(mutantmodel, "author_semester")`. Overall, this only explains 
`r r.sq(mutantmodel)` of the total variation, much less than for tests.

### Calculating a skill metric

I decided on a combination of quiz results and JUnit experience as a skill 
metric, as both have a significant positive effect on mutant quality, and a
possibly positive effect on test quality. Semester and Java experience have
a positive effect on test quality and a negative effect on mutant quality
and are therefore not included.

This stat is simply calculated as the mean of the normalized values of these
two variables. (Note TODO remove before end TODO: This happens within 
`load_data.R`) Then, players are sorted into LLM, low-skilled human (skill is
below the median), and high-skilled human (skill is above the median).





```{r}
deftests |>
  filter(!is.na(kill_rate)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_actor, fill = author_actor, y = kill_rate)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(fill = NULL, y = "Killrate", x = "Defender")
  
  
```

# Influence of experiment round

Note: Such diagrams are probably not necessary, now that we have the regression
model above.

Users played two different games:

- In both games, they played the same role, either attacker or defender.
- In one game, they played against another human, in the other one against
an LLM player
- In one game, they played on `ByteVector`, in the other one, on `CharRange`.


```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(author_llm_or_human == "Human") |>
  ggplot(aes(y = evasion_rate, x = round)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```




# Killrates

A "Killrate" is calculated for every single test. It describes the percentage of 
mutants within a specific population that would be killed by this test among 
those that are covered by this test.

"existing" and "future" mutants refers to those mutants within the same game
as the test that were submitted before/after the test was submitted.

```{r}

deftests |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(kill_rate, llm_kill_rate, human_kill_rate, existing_kill_rate, future_kill_rate),
    names_to = "kill_rate_type",
    values_to = "kill_rate_value"
  ) |>
  mutate(kill_rate_type = factor(kill_rate_type, 
                                 levels = c(
                                   "kill_rate", 
                                   "human_kill_rate", 
                                   "llm_kill_rate", 
                                   "existing_kill_rate",
                                   "future_kill_rate"),
                                 labels = c(
                                   "Total kill rate",
                                   "Against human mutants",
                                   "Against llm mutants",
                                   "Against existing mutants",
                                   "Against future mutants"
                                 ))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = kill_rate_value, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) + 
    geom_boxplot(position = "dodge") + 
    xlab("Defender") +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Kill rate", labels = percent) + 
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker", values = colors.actor) +
    facet_wrap( ~ kill_rate_type)
```

## Finding new mutants
How successful are tests in finding mutants that have previously been undetected?
This counts the absolute number of mutants, so there are no percentages.

Most tests only directly kill 0 or 1 mutants.

```{r}
deftests |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = fresh_killed_mutants, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  xlab("Defender") + 
  ylab("Number of killed mutants") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Attacker")

```

Comparing averages shows clearer results. For both classes, human-written
tests kill more hitherto surviving mutants. Tests also have kill more new
LLM-written mutants.

Possible explanations for this: Human defenders write fewer tests than LLM 
defenders, so every test has more mutants available to kill.

```{r}
deftests |>
  summarise(fresh_killed_mutants = mean(fresh_killed_mutants), .by = c(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, cut)) |>
  binary_mean_cols(fresh_killed_mutants, "t", with.percent = FALSE) +
  labs(y = "Average kills", title = "Fresh killed mutants")
```



# Evasion rate

An evasion rate is the equivalent of a kill rate for mutants: How many of the
tests in a specific population that cover this test could this mutant survive?

```{r}
mutants |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(evasion_rate, llm_evasion_rate, human_evasion_rate, existing_evasion_rate, future_evasion_rate),
    names_to = "evasion_rate_type",
    values_to = "evasion_rate_value"
  ) |>
  mutate(evasion_rate_type = factor(evasion_rate_type, 
                                 levels = c(
                                   "evasion_rate", 
                                   "human_evasion_rate", 
                                   "llm_evasion_rate", 
                                   "existing_evasion_rate",
                                   "future_evasion_rate"),
                                 labels = c(
                                   "Total evasion rate",
                                   "Against human tests",
                                   "Against llm tests",
                                   "Against existing tests",
                                   "Against future tests"
                                 ))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = evasion_rate_value, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) + 
    geom_boxplot(position = "dodge") + 
    xlab("Attacker") +
    scale_y_continuous(name = "Evasion rate", labels = percent) + 
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Defender", values = colors.actor) +
    facet_wrap( ~ evasion_rate_type)
```


# Points

## Points of individual tests

The following plots show the distribution of points for tests and mutants.
As we can see, most tests score very low, with some exceptionally high outliers.

```{r}
point_boxplot <- function(.data, author = "Author", opponent = "Opponent") {
  .data |>
    ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = points, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) + 
    geom_boxplot() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = opponent) +
    xlab(author) +
    ylab("Points") +
    facet_wrap( ~ cut)
}

deftests |>
  point_boxplot()
```

This plot shows the percentage of tests with at least one point. When playing
against an LLM attacker, humans and LLM defenders get at least one point
at almost the exact same rate, but against humans, human defenders score more
often.

```{r}
deftests |>
  mutate(has_points = points > 0) |>
  binary_mean_cols(has_points, "t") +
  ylab(NULL) +
  ggtitle("Tests with at least one point")
```
The average human-written tests scores higher than the average LLM-written test.
The difference is small (TODO significance?) in `CharRange`, larger in `ByteVector`.

```{r}
deftests |>
  group_by(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, cut) |>
  summarise(mean_points = mean(points)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = mean_points, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = mean_points |> round(2)), 
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    vjust = 1.5
    ) +
  xlab("Defender") +
  ylab("Points") +
  ggtitle("Average test points") + 
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker", values = colors.actor) +
  facet_wrap( ~ cut)
```

## Points of individual mutants

Same as with tests, mutant points are usually very low, with some outliers.

```{r}
mutants |>
  point_boxplot()
```
Humans are somewhat more successful in writing mutants that garner at least one
point. Getting at least a single point against a human defender seems to be much
easier for both LLM and human attackers, compared with an LLM defender.

```{r}
mutants |>
  mutate(has_points = points > 0) |>
  binary_mean_cols(has_points, "m") +
  ylab(NULL) +
  ggtitle("Mutants with at least one point")
```
In contrast, the average number of points is higher when playing against an
LLM defender compared to a human defender. Average mutant points are
generally higher for human attackers, especially in `ByteVector`.

```{r}
deftests |>
  group_by(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, cut) |>
  summarise(mean_points = mean(points)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = mean_points, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = mean_points |> round(2)), 
    position = position_dodge(0.9),
    vjust = 1.5
    ) +
  xlab("Attacker") +
  ylab("Points") +
  ggtitle("Average mutant points") + 
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Defender", values = colors.actor) +
  facet_wrap( ~ cut)
```


# Relationship between points and killrates

While there is no clear pattern for the relationship between the points
earned in-game by test and their total "kill-rate" against all mutants submitted
in the study, mutants that earn many points tend to have higher "evasion-rates"
against all tests submitted in the study.

Mutants that were declared as equivalent while not being killed by any test
were excluded from the sample.

```{r}
deftests |> 
  mutate(
    point_ntil = ntile(points, n = 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(point_ntil) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = kill_rate, x = factor(point_ntil), fill = author_llm_or_human)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Defender") + 
    ggtitle("Kill rates vs Points for tests") +
    xlab("Point deciles") + 
    ylab("Total kill rate") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)

```

```{r}
mutants |> 
  filter(!(!has_been_killed &declared_equivalent)) |>
  mutate(
    point_ntil = ntile(points, n = 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(point_ntil) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = evasion_rate, x = factor(point_ntil), fill = author_llm_or_human)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Attacker") + 
    ggtitle("Evasion rates vs Points for mutants") +
    xlab("Point deciles") + 
    ylab("Total evasion rate") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)
```

```{r}
ggplot(mutants, aes(x = points, y = evasion_rate)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(formula = y ~x, method = loess) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1), labels = percent, name = "Global evasion rate") + 
  xlab("Points")
```

# Submission timelines

These plots show the average number of tests/mutants submitted per minute per game.

We can see that LLM defenders submitted significantly more tests per minute than
human defenders, showing that the cooldown period was configured to be too low.

Submission rates for LLM defenders go down with time. It seems that the initial
"test suite" tests require re-generation less often than the uniquely written tests.

```{r}
timelineplot <- function(.data) {
  .data |>
  mutate(seconds_since_gamestart = floor(seconds_since_gamestart / 60)) |>
    rename(`Minutes since gamestart` = seconds_since_gamestart) |>
    mutate(
      part = as.numeric(ifelse(author_llm_or_human == "LLM",
                    1 / number_of_test_games[number_of_test_games$author_llm_or_human == "LLM","n"],
                    1 / number_of_test_games[number_of_test_games$author_llm_or_human == "Human","n"]
                    ))
    ) |>
    group_by(`Minutes since gamestart`, author_llm_or_human, cut) |>
    summarise(
      part = sum(part)
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Minutes since gamestart`, y = part, colour = author_llm_or_human)) +
    geom_line() +
    facet_wrap( ~ cut)
}

deftests |>
  timelineplot() +
  ylab("Test submissions per game and minute") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Defender")
```

Submission rates for mutants go down over time for both LLM and Human Attackers.
Since LLM attacker attempt to submit a new mutant every 30 seconds, this must
be related to higher rejection rates. A possible reason for that is the requirement
of mutants to be unique, there will be more collisions later in the game.

```{r}
mutants |>
  timelineplot() +
  ylab("Mutant submissions per game and minute") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Attacker")
```

# LLM messages until success

LLM players can try to fix their generated tests/mutants if they failed validation.
These plots show the number of successfully submitted tests/mutants per minute,
grouped by the number of messages to the LLM that were necessary for this submission.

Some tests have no directly associated number of messages. Those tests were generated
as part of the initial test suite and were successfully submitted on first try.


```{r}
deftests|>
  filter(author_llm_or_human == "LLM") |>
  mutate(number_of_messages = ifelse(is.na(number_of_messages), 0, number_of_messages)) |>
  mutate(number_of_messages = factor(number_of_messages,
                                     levels = c(0, 1,2,3,4),
                                     labels = c("Suite", "1", "2", "3", "4"))) |>
  mutate(seconds_since_gamestart = seconds_since_gamestart / 60) |>
  rename(`Minutes since gamestart` = seconds_since_gamestart) |>
  group_by(number_of_messages) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Minutes since gamestart`, colour = number_of_messages)) +
    geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 1) + 
    ylab("Tests per minute") +
    scale_colour_manual(name = "Number of messages", values = c("black", colors.quality)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ cut)
  
```

```{r}
mutants|>
  filter(author_llm_or_human == "LLM") |>
  mutate(number_of_messages = factor(number_of_messages,
                                     levels = c(0, 1,2,3,4),
                                     labels = c("Suite", "1", "2", "3", "4"))) |>
  mutate(seconds_since_gamestart = seconds_since_gamestart / 60) |>
  rename(`Minutes since gamestart` = seconds_since_gamestart) |>
  group_by(number_of_messages) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = `Minutes since gamestart`, colour = number_of_messages)) +
    geom_freqpoly(binwidth = 1) + 
    ylab("Mutants per minute") +
    scale_colour_manual(name = "Number of messages", values = c(colors.quality)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ cut)
```



# Turing tests

LLM-generated tests are almost never confused for human-written tests,
but mutants are hardly distinguishable.

```{r}
deftests |>
  filter(opponent_llm_or_human == "Human") |>
  group_by(game_id, author_username, opponent_opinion_human_or_ai, author_llm_or_human) |>
  mutate(opponent_opinion_human_or_ai = factor(opponent_opinion_human_or_ai, levels = 1:5, labels = interpretation.opponent_opinion_human_or_ai)) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = n, fill = opponent_opinion_human_or_ai)) + 
    geom_col(position = "fill", name = "Proportion") +
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker's guess", values = colors.opinion) +
    xlab("Defender") +
    ylab("Proportion") +
    ggtitle("Defender Turing test") + 
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)

```

```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(opponent_llm_or_human == "Human") |>
  group_by(game_id, author_username, opponent_opinion_human_or_ai, author_llm_or_human) |>
  mutate(opponent_opinion_human_or_ai = factor(opponent_opinion_human_or_ai, levels = 1:5, labels = interpretation.opponent_opinion_human_or_ai)) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = n, fill = opponent_opinion_human_or_ai)) + 
    geom_col(position = "fill", name = "Proportion") +
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Defender's guess", values = colors.opinion) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
    xlab("Attacker") +
    ylab("Proportion") + 
    ggtitle("Attacker Turing test")
```

# Stillborn mutants

A stillborn mutant is a mutant that was killed by a test that was already in the game.

## Proportions
This plot shows the proportions of stillborn mutants within a population.
We can see that LLM-generated mutants are more likely to be stillborn than
human-written mutants, and that mutants are much more likely to be killed
on submission when playing against an LLM player compared to a human player.

This last point can possibly be explained by the fact that LLM defenders first 
generate a complete test suite before writing individual tests.

```{r}
mutants |>
  binary_mean_cols(is_stillborn, "m") +
  ylab("Stillborn") +
  ggtitle("Percentages of stillborn mutants")


```
There are, however, only very slight differences in total evasion rates
between stillborn and not-stillborn mutants.

```{r}
ggplot(data = mutants, aes(x = is_stillborn, y = evasion_rate, fill = author_llm_or_human)) +
  geom_boxplot(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker", values = colors.actor) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, name = "Evasion rate") +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Not stillborn", "Stillborn"),) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  ggtitle("Total evasion rates of stillborn and not-stillborn mutants")
```



# Equivalences
The following plots show the percentage of mutants that could not be killed by any test
in the entire study among their respective population.

For the purpose of this analysis, we assume that all mutants that could not be killed
by any test in the study are actually equivalent. 

We can see that at least 20% of human-written mutants that were declared as equivalent
after being claimed as equivalent by another human were actually killable. 

In contrast, at least 57% of LLM-written tests that 
were accepted as equivalent after being claimed as equivalent by a human were
killable. 

In LLM-vs-LLM-games, almost every equivalent test was marked as equivalent.
This is because in LLM-vs-LLM games, after the normal time ends, players
stop the normal test/mutant submission, the defender claims every surviving
mutant as equivalent, and the attacker is given the opportunity to defend
against that. This procedure was chosen because without it, many equivalent
tests with just shy of 10 points would in total provide a massive point 
advantage to the attacker. LLM-vs-LLM games are therefore not comparable to the
other combinations.
```{r}

mutants |>
  group_by(
    author_llm_or_human,
    declared_equivalent,
    opponent_llm_or_human
  ) |>
  summarise(
    not_killed = mean(!has_been_killed)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    opponent_llm_or_human = paste(opponent_llm_or_human, "Defender")
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = declared_equivalent, y = not_killed, fill = author_llm_or_human)
    ) +
    geom_col(position = "dodge") +
    geom_text(aes(
      label = percent(not_killed),
      vjust = -0.4
      ), position = position_dodge(0.9)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ opponent_llm_or_human,) + 
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, name = "Equivalent mutants") + 
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Not declared\n equivalent", "Declared equivalent")) +
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker", values = colors.actor) +
    xlab(NULL)

  
```
```{r}
mutants |>
  group_by(
    author_llm_or_human,
    opponent_llm_or_human,
    has_been_killed
  ) |>
  summarise(
    declared_equivalent = mean(declared_equivalent)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    opponent_llm_or_human = paste(opponent_llm_or_human, "Defender")
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(x = has_been_killed, y = declared_equivalent, fill = author_llm_or_human)
    ) +
    geom_col(position = "dodge") +
    facet_wrap( ~ opponent_llm_or_human,) + 
    ylab("Mutants declared as equivalent") +
    scale_percentage_bars() +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Equivalent", "Not equivalent")) +
    scale_fill_manual(name = "Attacker", values = colors.actor) +
    ggtitle("Equivalent mutants") + 
    xlab(NULL)
```

# Line coverage

This plot shows the number of lines being covered by a test.
LLM generated tests cover slightly more lines than human written tests.

```{r}
deftests |>

  facet_wrap( ~ cut) +

  ylab("Covered lines") +

```
For mutants, the difference is more pronounced. Most human mutants only change a
single line, while LLM mutants often change multiple lines.

However, this counts all changes, including changes to comments which were
illegal for human players, but permitted to LLM players.

```{r}
mutants |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human, y = number_mutated_lines, fill = opponent_llm_or_human)) +

  xlab("Attacker") +
```

## Which lines were covered and mutated?

The following plots show which lines were covered and mutated by tests and
mutants, respectively. We can see some interesting patterns: There are only
minor differences depending on the attacker, LLM defenders were much more
likely to cover a collection of lines at the end of CharRange, and LLM 
attackers focused a majority of their attacks on a single cluster of lines,
while human attackers (as a whole) distributed their attacks more evenly across
the CuT.
```{r}

coverage_plot <- function(.data, type) {
  if (! type %in% c("t", "m")) {
    stop("type must be t or m")
  }
  old_lines <- if (type == "t") "lines_covered" else "mutatedlines"
  old_id <- if (type == "t") "test_id" else "mutant_id"
  
  .data |>
    rename(.lines = !!sym(old_lines)) |>
    rename(.id = !!sym(old_id)) |>
    select(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, .lines, .id) |>
    separate_longer_delim(.lines, delim=",") |>
    unique() |>
    mutate(linecount = 1) |>
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = .lines, 
      values_from = linecount, 
      names_prefix = "lineno_",
      values_fill = 0
      ) |>
    summarise(across(starts_with("lineno_"), mean), .by = c(
      "author_llm_or_human",
      "opponent_llm_or_human"
    )) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("lineno_"),
      names_to = "line_number",
      names_prefix = "lineno_",
      values_to = "line_mean",
      names_transform = as.integer
    ) |>
    mutate(
      author_llm_or_human = paste(author_llm_or_human, if (type == "t") "Defender" else "Attacker"),
      opponent_llm_or_human = paste(opponent_llm_or_human, if (type == "m") "Defender" else "Attacker")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = line_number, y = line_mean)) +
    geom_col() +
    facet_grid(author_llm_or_human ~ opponent_llm_or_human) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = percent)
}

deftests |>
  filter(cut == "CharRange") |>
  coverage_plot("t") +
  labs(title = "Coverage for CharRange", y = "Tests that cover this line", x = "Line number")
```

```{r}
deftests |>
  filter(cut == "ByteVector") |>
  coverage_plot("t") +
  labs(title = "Coverage for ByteVector", y = "Tests that cover this line", x = "Line number")
```

```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(cut == "CharRange") |>
  coverage_plot("m") +
  labs(title = "Mutations for CharRange", y = "Mutants that change this line", x = "Line number")
```

```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(cut == "ByteVector") |>
  coverage_plot("m") +
  labs(title = "Mutations for ByteVector", y = "Mutants that change this line", x = "Line number")
```

## Which methods were covered and mutated?

The plots above are difficult to parse, so we will map the line numbers to methods.

```{r}
CharRange_mapping <- function(l) {
  l <- as.integer(l)
  case_when(
    l < 6 ~ "Documentation",
    l < 8 ~ "Class declaration",
    l < 18 ~ "Fields",
    l < 45 ~ "Constructor",
    l < 57 ~ "is()",
    l < 69 ~ "isNot()",
    l < 82 ~ "isIn()",
    l < 95 ~ "isNotIn()",
    l < 106 ~ "getStart()",
    l < 115 ~ "getEnd()",
    l < 127 ~ "isNegated()",
    l < 139 ~ "contains(char)",
    l < 161 ~ "contains(CharRange)",
    l < 184 ~ "equals()",
    l < 194 ~ "hashCode()",
    l <= 217 ~ "toString()"
  )
}

ByteVector_mapping <- function(l) {
  l <- as.integer(l)
  case_when(
    l < 6 ~ "Documentation",
    l < 8 ~ "Class declaration",
    l < 18 ~ "Fields",
    l < 26 ~ "ByteVector()",
    l < 36 ~ "ByteVector(int)",
    l < 53 ~ "putByte()",
    l < 73 ~ "put11()",
    l < 92 ~ "putShort()",
    l < 113 ~ "put12()",
    l < 134 ~ "putInt()",
    l < 161 ~ "putLong()",
    l < 226 ~ "putUTF8()",
    l < 248 ~ "putByteArray()",
    l <= 262 ~ "enlarge()"
  )
}

method_coverage_plot <- function(.data, type) {
  if (! type %in% c("t", "m")) {
    stop("type must be t or m")
  }
  old_lines <- if (type == "t") "lines_covered" else "mutatedlines"
  old_id <- if (type == "t") "test_id" else "mutant_id"
  mapping <- if (.data[1,"cut"] == "ByteVector") ByteVector_mapping else CharRange_mapping
  #TODO: Would be a bit more elegant to do this in every row, to allow for
  # mixed input
  
  .data |>
    rename(.lines = !!sym(old_lines)) |>
    rename(.id = !!sym(old_id)) |>
    select(author_llm_or_human, opponent_llm_or_human, .lines, .id) |>
    separate_longer_delim(.lines, delim=",") |>
    mutate(.lines = mapping(.lines)) |>
    unique() |>
    mutate(linecount = 1) |>
    pivot_wider(
      names_from = .lines, 
      values_from = linecount, 
      names_prefix = "lineno_",
      values_fill = 0
      ) |>
    summarise(across(starts_with("lineno_"), mean), .by = c(
      "author_llm_or_human",
      "opponent_llm_or_human"
    )) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols = starts_with("lineno_"),
      names_to = "line_number",
      names_prefix = "lineno_",
      values_to = "line_mean",
      names_transform = factor
    ) |>
    mutate(
      author_llm_or_human = paste(author_llm_or_human, if (type == "t") "Defender" else "Attacker"),
      opponent_llm_or_human = paste(opponent_llm_or_human, if (type == "m") "Defender" else "Attacker")
      ) |>
    ggplot(aes(y = line_number, x = line_mean)) +
    geom_col() +
    facet_grid(opponent_llm_or_human ~ author_llm_or_human) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = percent)
}
```


There are no remarkable differences between human and LLM defenders when it comes
to coverage. Generally speaking, methods are covered more often by the LLM
defenders, and `CharRange.toString()` is covered much more often than by Human
defenders.

```{r}
deftests |>
  filter(cut == "CharRange") |>
  method_coverage_plot("t") +
  labs(title = "Tests for CharRange", x = "Tests that cover this method", y = "Method name")
```

For `ByteVector`, the only difference that jumps to the eye is that LLM 
defenders are much more likely to use the parameterized constructor instead
of the default constructor. A possible explanation for that is that the
convenience of a shorter name does not matter for the LLM, but does so for the
humans.

```{r}
deftests |>
  filter(cut == "ByteVector") |>
  method_coverage_plot("t") +
  labs(title = "Tests for ByteVectore", x = "Tests that cover this method", y = "Method name")
```
Behavior between human and LLM attackers, however, differs much more extremely.
For `CharRange`, both human and LLM attackers mutated the method 
`contains(CharRange)`, which is the most complex method of the class, in a
plurality of their submissions. LLM attackers concentrated on this method far
more, however, to the point that almost 60% of all LLM-generated mutants in
games against humans target this method.

```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(cut == "CharRange") |>
  method_coverage_plot("m") +
  labs(title = "Mutations for CharRange", x = "Mutants that change this method", y = "Method name")
```

For `ByteVector`, this effect is even more extreme, reaching almost 80% for the
most complex method `putUTF8()`. As in `CharRange`, the effect is stronger
when matched against a human.

```{r}
mutants |>
  filter(cut == "ByteVector") |>
  method_coverage_plot("m") +
  labs(title = "Mutations for ByteVector", x = "Mutants that change this method", y = "Method name")
```

Both classes have one method that is clearly much more complex than the other
methods, it would be interesting to know how the LLM would act in classes where
the complexity is more evenly distributed.

## Winrates

Generally, attackers have a very high win rate, at about 80%.

In `ByteVector`, attackers win every single game except in LLM-vs-LLM setups,
while winrates in `CharRange` are more balanced. 

In LLM-vs-LLM games, winrates for defenders are much higher than in all
other setups. 
This difference could be the effect of a unique mechanic of LLM-vs-LLM games,
where all surviving mutants are claimed as equivalent. As seen above, LLM
attackers are much more likely to fail to prove that a mutant is not equivalent,
resulting in many more lost points due to lost equivalence duels.

(Defender winrates and attacker winrates are essentially the same data,
reversed. There is not a single draw in the data set.) 

```{r}
games <- attacker_games |>
  inner_join(defender_games, join_by(game_id, cut, round), suffix = c(".attacker", ".defender"))|>
  select(!starts_with("opponent"))

games |>
  group_by(author_llm_or_human.attacker, author_llm_or_human.defender, cut) |>
  summarise(
    defender_winrate = mean(points.defender > points.attacker)
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human.defender, fill = author_llm_or_human.attacker, 
             y = defender_winrate, label = percent(defender_winrate))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Attacker") + 
  xlab("Defender") +
  ggtitle("Defender winrates") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, name = "Defender winrate") +
  geom_text(position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = 1.5) +
  facet_wrap( ~ cut)
```

```{r}
games |>
  group_by(author_llm_or_human.attacker, author_llm_or_human.defender, cut) |>
  summarise(
    attacker_winrate = mean(points.defender < points.attacker)
    ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = author_llm_or_human.attacker, fill = author_llm_or_human.defender, 
             y = attacker_winrate, label = percent(attacker_winrate))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colors.actor, name = "Defender") + 
  xlab("Attacker") +
  ggtitle("Attacker winrates") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, name = "Attacker winrate") +
  geom_text(position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = 1.5) +
```


# Failures

Not all tests and mutants that are submitted by human or by the LLM players are
valid. Some of them fail the initial validation phase: In this case, the 
submissions never enter the database. For human submissions, this means that we
have no data whatsoever, for LLM submissions, that we have to parse the messages
of failed LLM conversations for more information. Initial validation fails if
one of the various validation rules for CodeDefenders is violated (for example,
if a test contains more than 2 assertions, or if there are calls to `System` or 
`Random`) or if the submission cannot be parsed by a Java Parser.

Two types of failures can be directly analyzed: Submissions that can be parsed, but
not compiled, and tests that fail on the original class.

## Validation errors for LLMs

While no such data exists for human submissions, we can extract the replies to
the LLM for rejected submissions. There are some caveats to consider:

The validation system in the CodeDefenders build used during the study is
imprecise and often buggy. This has since been fixed, but many of the categories
are overly broad and unspecific. I assume that this has also influenced LLM
behaviour. For example, adding a loop to a test is illegal in CodeDefenders.
The message that is sent back to the LLM only specifies that this loop is an
"Invalid statement", without any explanation as to why. In some cases, the
rejection reason remains empty.

These messages also do not cover the last, unsuccessful attempt of an LLM
to generate a submission, since there will not be an answer to the last attempt,
instead, a new conversation is started.

Also, only one error message is returned to the LLM, so if a submission fails
for one reason, we cannot know if it would have failed for other reasons.

Still, we have can garner some insights. 

### Test rejections

Test submissions are primarily rejected because of "Invalid statements".
These statements, like loops, ternary operators, if-statements and logical
comparisons would not actually be invalid in a real-world test suite,
but are forbidden in CodeDefenders. This error type could 
potentially be improved in future iterations by a more detailed system prompt.

Only 51% of all messages with this error belong to a conversation that
eventually succeeds. Better error messages that explain what kind of expression
is not allowed could also help.

The same is true for "prohibited calls", which refers to calls to `System.*`,
Random number generators, IO, etc., with an eventual success rate of only 44%.

For compilation errors and tests that fail on the original, the eventual success
rates are high in comparison, with 72.2% and 79.5% eventual success rates,
respectively.

There are significant differences between the classes for which these tests
were generated. LLMs were far more likely to generate invalid statements for
`CharRange` compared to `ByteVector`, while the number of compile errors is
smaller. It is, as noted above, possible however that some of those tests rejected for invalid
statements would have been uncompilable anyway. Eventual success rates are 
usually higher for `CharRange`. 

The other failure reasons have a much lower incidence.



```{r}
all_messages |>
  filter(startsWith(as.character(rejection_reason), "Test")) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(rejection_reason, cut)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = rejection_reason, y = n, x = "")) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Rejection reasons for defender tests",
       x = NULL,
       y = "Number of failed attemps",
       fill = "Rejection reason") +
  geom_text(aes(label = after_stat(y)), position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ cut)
```

```{r}
all_messages |>
  filter(startsWith(as.character(rejection_reason), "Test")) |>
  summarise(is_success = mean(is_success), .by = c(rejection_reason, cut)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = is_success, fill = rejection_reason)) +
  scale_percentage_bars() +
  labs(title = "Eventual success rates for rejected tests", 
       y = "Eventual success percentage",
       fill = "Rejection reason",
       x = NULL) +
  facet_wrap( ~ cut)
  
```

### Mutants

The vast majority of rejected mutants are rejected because an identical mutant
already exists. 79% of them could eventually be submitted.

It might be worth considering if it could be worthwhile to supply the LLM with a
sample of the most often repeated mutants and tell it specifically to do 
something different.

From the other reasons, only "Mutant has prohibited operations" is present in
significant numbers. More detailed error messages could provide more interesting
data, but the eventual success rate is still much higher than for most test
failures, at 93%.



```{r}
all_messages |>
  filter(startsWith(as.character(rejection_reason), "Mutant")) |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = c(rejection_reason, cut)) |>
  ggplot(aes(fill = rejection_reason, y = n, x = "")) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Rejection reasons for attacker tests",
       x = NULL,#"Conversation is eventually successful",
       y = "Number of failed attemps",
       fill = "Rejection reason") +
  geom_text(aes(label = after_stat(y)), position = position_dodge(0.9), vjust = -0.2) +
  facet_wrap( ~ cut)
```
```{r}
all_messages |>
  filter(startsWith(as.character(rejection_reason), "Mutant")) |>
  summarise(is_success = mean(is_success), .by = c(rejection_reason, cut)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = "", y = is_success, fill = rejection_reason)) +
  scale_percentage_bars(vjust = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Eventual success rates for rejected mutants", 
       y = "Eventual success percentage",
       fill = "Rejection reason",
       x = NULL) +
  facet_grid(cut ~ .)
```


## Tests

For humans, there is only a small difference in compilation rates between
playing against another human and playing against an LLM. LLM players, however,
submit a much higher percentage of uncompilable tests when playing against a
human than when playing against another LLM. I did not expect any significant 
difference at all, and I have no explanation for this. TODO

```{r}
all_tests |>
  filter(!is_equivalence_test) |>
  mutate(uncompilable = !is_compiled) |>
  binary_mean_cols(y = uncompilable, type = "t") +
  ggtitle("Uncompilable tests") +
  ylab("Uncompilable")
```

Curiously, the failure rates of tests against the CuT, when written by humans,
are much higher for `ByteVector` than for `CharRange`, while the compilation
rates are higher for `CharRange` than for `ByteVector`. For both variables,
high rates suggest difficulties for human testers in understanding the source 
code, but they point in opposite directions.

For `CharRange`, LLMs and Humans achieved similar failure rates of about
10%, but for `ByteVector`, Human failure rates reached around 34%, while LLM
failure rates only reached about 4%.

```{r}
all_tests |>
  filter(!is_equivalence_test) |>
  binary_mean_cols(y = fails_against_cut, type = "t") +
  ggtitle("Tests that fail against the CuT") +
  ylab("Failure rate")
```

## Mutants

Once the initial validation was passed, only very few LLM-generated mutants
failed to compile, in fact, only a single LLM-generated mutant didn't compile
for `ByteVector`. As with tests, human-written mutants failed to compile
more often when matched against other humans, but the effect is small.
TODO Quantify!

```{r}
all_mutants |>
  mutate(uncompilable = !is_compiled) |>
  binary_mean_cols(y = uncompilable, type = "m") +
  ggtitle("Uncompilable mutants") +
  ylab("Uncompilable")
```
